"Thursday night, eleven o'clock, the deal we lost, and we ended up shouting about invoices," Jahnavi said, stirring her tea. "Then Monday, same thing."
"You're saying it's my fault?" Akash's shoulders went stiff.
"No. I'm saying look at the clock. We're wrecked, and I get sharp when I'm tired. So do you, honestly."
Akash let out a breath. "Yeah. Okay."
"So the hard talks wait. Saturday mornings, tea, before the laptops. Not on the heels of a lost deal."
"And if something can't wait?"
"Then we say it in one line and leave the rest for Saturday."
"Fine. Try it once."
Two Saturdays later they went through the invoices in twenty minutes, and neither raised their voice.

I noticed the pattern before Pallavi did. Our worst fights about the startup always happened after ten at night, usually on a day when a customer had said no. We'd both be tired and bruised, and some small thing, a missed email or a price quote, would turn into "you never" and "you always".
One Tuesday, after a fight about a discount that went on till 1 am, I lay awake and thought: we don't disagree more at night. We just defend harder when we're tired. The same topic on a good morning would be a ten-minute talk.
The next day I said, "What if we ban co-founder arguments after 9 pm? Anything big waits for Saturday morning, over tea, at your place." Pallavi laughed but agreed.
The first Saturday, the discount question took twelve minutes. We didn't raise our voices once.
— Chaitanya

Coach's notes, 14 March.
Vidya and Kiran, founders of the solar-pump rental startup. Third session. They came in after a bad week: two farmer cooperatives had cancelled. Within five minutes they were arguing about who should have followed up. Vidya said Kiran "always drops things"; Kiran said Vidya "never lets anything go".
I stopped them and asked when these fights usually happen. They looked at each other. Kiran said, "Late, after a bad day." Vidya nodded. "On the phone, at 11 pm, when a deal falls through."
Before leaving, they set a new rule themselves: no business arguments after 8 pm or on the day of a lost sale. Anything serious gets written down and discussed on Saturday morning over tea, once they have both slept. I'll ask at the next session whether it held.

qa.q: When did Vidya say the fights usually happened?
qa.a: "On the phone, at 11 pm, when a deal falls through."

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling when accused of always dropping things?
qa.a: Kiran likely felt stung and defensive, which is why the reply was that Vidya never lets anything go.

qa.q: Why is a Saturday morning over tea a better time?
qa.a: Both are rested and not raw from a lost sale, so they are less defensive and can actually solve the problem.

qa.q: How does the coach see the change in the pair?
qa.a: The coach sees them spot their own pattern and set the rule themselves, and plans to check next session whether it held.
